Schools and movements

Functionalism

Asking what the mind is for in adaptation.

What does it propose?The important question is not what the mind is made of but what it is for: how it helps the organism adapt to its environment.
What does it study?Habits, attention, learning, emotions, individual differences, child development and animal behaviour.
How does it study it?Varied methods: introspection, observation, animal experiments, mental tests and applied studies in schools and workplaces.
Who took part?William James, John Dewey, James Rowland Angell and Harvey Carr in Chicago, James McKeen Cattell and Edward Thorndike at Columbia, Mary Whiton Calkins and G. Stanley Hall.
What remains?Applied psychology (educational, occupational, clinical), the study of individual differences and the evolutionary perspective. Many ideas passed into behaviourism and cognitive psychology.
What is debated?It was never a closed school with a defined programme, which made it flexible but hard to pin down. Its concept of consciousness remained vague to its critics.

Context

Functionalism was born in the United States in a climate shaped by Darwin and by philosophical pragmatism, which judged ideas by their practical consequences. Its starting point was William James's Principles of Psychology (1890), which described consciousness as a continuous, personal stream, always in the service of action.

Key ideas

  • The mind as adaptation: consciousness exists because it helps us survive, especially in new situations where habits are not enough.
  • The reflex arc as a circuit: in 1896 John Dewey criticised the idea of a separate stimulus and response; perceiving and acting form a coordinated cycle.
  • Mind and body in relation: in 1907 James Rowland Angell defined functional psychology as the study of mental operations and their role in the relation between organism and environment.
  • Usefulness: psychology should help improve education, work and everyday life.

An example

In 1896 Dewey founded an experimental school at the University of Chicago where children learned by doing: cooking, building or growing a garden. It was the direct application of a psychology that saw thinking as a tool for solving real problems.

Historical importance and current support

As a school it dissolved around 1930, but largely because it won: almost all later psychology is "functionalist" in the sense of asking what the processes it studies are for. Educational, occupational and evolutionary psychology are its direct heirs.

Habit and the stream of consciousness

William James wrote famous pages on habit, which he called "the enormous fly-wheel of society": it saves us effort but also binds us. And he described consciousness not as a sum of elements but as a continuous, changing stream, an expression that also influenced literature.

Education and individual differences

Functionalism was interested in how the mind adapts, which led to the study of children, animals and differences between people. In 1896 John Dewey founded an experimental school in Chicago where children learnt by doing. James McKeen Cattell promoted mental tests. Mary Whiton Calkins, a student of James, developed a psychology of the self.

A legacy without a name

Functionalism did not disappear through defeat but because its ideas became part of the common sense of American psychology: studying what behaviour is for, applying psychology to school and work, and accepting varied methods. That is why it is sometimes said that all psychologists today are, in part, functionalists.

A school's historical importance and the current scientific support for its ideas are different things: we explain them separately.

References

  1. James, W. (1890). The Principles of Psychology. Nueva York: Henry Holt.
  2. Dewey, J. (1896). The reflex arc concept in psychology. Psychological Review, 3(4), 357–370.
  3. Angell, J. R. (1907). The province of functional psychology. Psychological Review, 14(2), 61–91.
